verdicts.reason: Both score whether the document properly cites its governing statutory/regulatory authority; the codification and executive-order clauses are incidental elaborations of one authority-citation concept.
Both measure whether an NPRM/notice was published with the required APA and Federal Register content (authority, substance/issues, procedural details), enumerating largely the same elements.

X requires substantive engagement with the agency's analytical documents (RIA/RFA/EIS) and its assumptions, while Y scores specificity/format/actionable asks, so a targeted comment with no analytic engagement scores high on Y and low on X.
Both measure whether the analysis identifies who bears costs and who receives benefits across groups; Y merely spells out the disaggregation categories.

X scores identification and targeting of the proceeding and sections, whereas Y additionally requires factual data, authorities, and legal weight, which a well-targeted but evidence-free comment would lack.
Both score the completeness and transparency of PRA information-collection burden estimates (respondents, frequency, hours per response, totals, associated costs).

Both score whether the Federal Register document carries its full complement of required structural elements and metadata (agency, RIN/docket, CFR parts, summary, authority citations, contact, availability).
Both ask whether the commenter supplied its own numeric compliance-cost figure together with the basis for it; the wording differs but the target is one concept.
Both ask whether the comment offers a concrete, adoptable alternative regulatory design rather than mere objection.
Both measure whether the comment pinpoints the docket and the exact provisions it addresses; the secondary 'give reasons' clause does not change the underlying targeting/identification construct.

Y is confined to defining covered conduct and contexts of sex discrimination/harassment, while X also governs authority, access to sex-segregated programs and facilities, and state-federal interpretive conflicts.
X scores engagement with the proposal's questions and text, while Y is a broader gestalt adding timeliness, counter-evidence, proposed alternatives, and quantitative content that X does not require.
X targets analytic identification of disproportionate impacts using EJ screening tools, while Y targets mitigation, community engagement, and embedding EJ into permitting and program design.
Both score the quality, completeness, and transparency of PRA ICR burden estimates and their standard breakdown components.

X is environmental-justice program design and mitigation with community data gathering, while Y is general distributional/equity analysis across subgroups; a rule can do one well and the other not at all.

X scores whether the SIP addresses required elements and area/regional program obligations, while Y scores stringency, equivalency, enforceability, and approvability criteria, so a complete-but-weakened SIP would split the two scores.

Y is narrowly about authority citations and CFR codification, whereas X scores the whole document's structural elements, metadata, signatures, and contact/IBR statements, of which citations are only one part.
Both score readability through organization: summary up front, headed sections, logical flow, and presentation that makes the comment easy to use.
First-hand operational experience in the regulated activity is unrelated to the intensity of expressed approval or disapproval; a purely emotional comment has one and not the other.

Both score identification of PRA-covered collections plus the objective breakdown and total of estimated burden; the need/opportunity-cost clauses are elaborations of the same estimate-quality concept.
Citing CFR provisions is a formal referencing property, while arguing the rule exceeds statutory authority is a substantive legal claim; either can appear without the other.
Y is specifically engagement with the RIA/economic analysis, while X is a broad comment-quality umbrella covering timeliness, specificity, alternatives, and evidence beyond economic analysis.

X scores responsiveness to the questions the agency solicited, while Y also demands engagement with the regulatory text and supporting analyses, so a comment answering only the posed questions splits the two.

X emphasizes procedural steps (NOI/scoping, draft/final/supplemental issuance, participation, Record of Decision), whereas Y emphasizes content adequacy and thresholds (EIS vs FONSI, categorical exclusions, required content elements, ESA coordination).

Both score institutional Title IX grievance procedures against the same procedural-safeguard checklist (notice, hearings/cross-examination, evidence standards, training, informal resolution, recordkeeping).
Both score whether distributional consequences across groups are made explicit and treated as decision-relevant; the equity framing names the same measurement.
Both score transparency of mass-comment campaigns: disclosing sponsors/funding, documenting campaign design, and detecting astroturfing or duplication.

X scores whether assertions are checkable and cited, while Y additionally scores argumentation craft (structure, signal-to-noise, anticipating and rebutting counterarguments), which a well-cited but unstructured comment lacks.
Both score whether claims rest on verifiable, credible, properly cited sources that a reader could check.
X scores the quality and methodology of the burden estimate itself, while Y scores whether burden was minimized and comment invited on reducing it, especially for small entities.
Both score coordination and harmonization across agencies and jurisdictions to avoid duplication and maintain consistency.
Both score the required content, structure, authority/signature blocks, and formatting conventions of Federal Register rulemaking documents.
